problems.subject: Discrete Mathematics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Counts a choice from mutually exclusive categories using the sum principle.
problems.title: Apply the sum principle to exclusive choices

student_facing.problem_statement: A snack counter offers 3 sandwich choices and 2 soup choices. A learner will choose exactly one item, either one sandwich or one soup. How many different choices are available? Explain why addition is appropriate.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: The sandwich and soup options are distinct, and exactly one item is selected.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: 3+2=5 different choices.
step_by_step_solution: There are 3 ways to choose a sandwich.
There are 2 ways to choose a soup.
The categories are mutually exclusive because exactly one item is selected.
By the sum principle, total choices are 3+2=5.
formulas_definitions_theorems: If alternatives are mutually exclusive, add their counts.
The sum principle counts a choice from one of several disjoint categories.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Identifies the two disjoint categories, adds their counts, and states the exactly-one condition that makes the categories exclusive.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: Listing the five individual choices is acceptable.

common_errors.misconception: Multiplying 3×2
corrective_followups: Are you choosing one sandwich and one soup, or one item from either category?
Would multiplication count pairs of items?

common_errors.misconception: Adding when the learner may choose one of each
corrective_followups: What does the phrase “exactly one item” require?
Would the categories still be mutually exclusive if two items could be selected?

problems.subject: Discrete Mathematics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Counts assignments to two distinct roles where order and role identity matter.
problems.title: Count ordered officer assignments

student_facing.problem_statement: Five candidates are eligible for chairperson and secretary. No person may hold both roles. How many different officer assignments are possible?
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Chairperson and secretary are different roles. One candidate is selected for each role.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: 5×4=20 assignments.
step_by_step_solution: Choose the chairperson in 5 ways.
After that choice, 4 candidates remain for secretary.
By the multiplication principle, there are 5·4=20 assignments.
Changing who holds which role creates a different assignment.
formulas_definitions_theorems: The number of ordered selections of r distinct objects from n is P(n,r)=n!/(n−r)!.
The multiplication principle counts successive choices.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Recognizes that roles are distinct, reduces the second choice by one, and multiplies the available choices.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: An ordered list of role assignments is acceptable if it accounts for all 20 possibilities.

common_errors.misconception: Using C(5,2)=10
corrective_followups: Would swapping the chairperson and secretary produce the same assignment?
Are you selecting an unordered pair or filling distinct roles?

common_errors.misconception: Using 5×5 and allowing one person to hold both roles
corrective_followups: What restriction applies after the first person is selected?
How many candidates remain?

problems.subject: Discrete Mathematics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Uses combinations when order does not distinguish outcomes.
problems.title: Count unordered selections

student_facing.problem_statement: A study group must select 2 learners from 6 volunteers. How many different two-person groups can be formed? Explain why order does not matter.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: No leadership roles are assigned. Selecting A then B is the same group as selecting B then A.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

step_by_step_solution: There are 6·5=30 ordered ways to select two different learners.
Each unordered group is counted twice, once in each order.
Divide by 2!: 30/2=15.
Equivalently, use C(6,2)=15.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Combinations count selections where order does not matter.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Identifies the selection as unordered and divides out the two possible orderings.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A systematic list or a combination formula is acceptable.

common_errors.misconception: Using 6×5=30 as the final answer
corrective_followups: Does the same two-person group appear in both orders?
How many orderings represent one group?

common_errors.misconception: Using 6² and allowing repeated selection
corrective_followups: Can the same learner be selected twice?
How many volunteers remain after one learner is selected?

problems.subject: Discrete Mathematics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Counts a restricted committee by subtracting the no-qualifying-member case from all committees.
problems.title: Count committees with at least one of two members

student_facing.problem_statement: A committee of 3 is selected from 6 candidates. Two candidates, Ana and Ben, are designated representatives. How many committees contain at least one of Ana or Ben?
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: All candidates are distinct; committees have no assigned roles; Ana and Ben may both be selected.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

step_by_step_solution: Count all 3-person committees: C(6,3)=20.
A committee containing neither Ana nor Ben must be chosen from the other 4 candidates: C(4,3)=4.
Subtract the excluded committees: 20−4=16.
The complement method counts committees with at least one designated representative, including those with both.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Number with at least one of a specified group = total−number with none.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Defines the complement correctly, counts all committees and those containing neither designated candidate, and subtracts.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: Separate cases with exactly one designated member and both designated members are acceptable if counted without overlap.

common_errors.misconception: Counting committees with exactly one representative instead of at least one
corrective_followups: Does the phrase “at least one” include committees with both?
Which complement excludes both representatives?

common_errors.misconception: Subtracting C(2,3) for the excluded group
corrective_followups: If neither Ana nor Ben is selected, how many candidates remain available?
How many ways can three be chosen from those four?

problems.difficulty_rationale: Counts distinct arrangements when identical letters are indistinguishable.
problems.title: Arrange a word with repeated letters

student_facing.problem_statement: How many distinct arrangements can be made from all five letters of the word LEVEL? Explain why a simple 5! count overcounts.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: The letters are L, E, V, E, L. The two Ls are identical and the two Es are identical.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: 5!/(2!2!)=30 distinct arrangements.
step_by_step_solution: If all five letters were distinct, there would be 5! arrangements.
Swapping the two identical Ls does not create a new word, so divide by 2!.
Swapping the two identical Es also does not create a new word, so divide by another 2!.
The number of distinct arrangements is 120/4=30.
formulas_definitions_theorems: For n objects with repeated groups of sizes n₁,n₂,…, the number of distinct arrangements is n!/(n₁!n₂!…).
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Identifies both repeated-letter groups and divides by each group's internal permutations.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A position-by-position counting argument that avoids duplicate arrangements is acceptable.

common_errors.misconception: Using 5! without correcting for repeated letters
corrective_followups: Do the two Ls create different visible arrangements when swapped?
How many permutations of identical copies produce the same word?

common_errors.misconception: Dividing by only one 2!
corrective_followups: Which letters occur twice?

problems.difficulty_rationale: Uses complementary counting to handle a forbidden-adjacency arrangement condition.
problems.title: Count arrangements with two books not adjacent

student_facing.problem_statement: Five distinct books are arranged on a shelf. Two particular books, A and B, must not be adjacent. How many arrangements satisfy the condition? Show the total count and the excluded count.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: All five books are distinct, and left-to-right order matters.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

step_by_step_solution: Count all arrangements of five distinct books: 5!=120.
For arrangements where A and B are adjacent, treat the pair as one block.
There are four objects to arrange: the AB block and the other three books, giving 4! orders.
Within the block, A and B can be ordered as AB or BA, giving 2 choices.
Adjacent arrangements total 4!·2=48.
Subtract: 120−48=72.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Complementary counting: desired count=total−excluded count.
A and B as one block produce 4! arrangements, with 2 internal orders.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Counts all arrangements, models the adjacent pair as a block, includes both internal orders, and subtracts the excluded cases.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A gap method placing the other three books first and choosing two nonadjacent gaps is acceptable if counted correctly.

common_errors.misconception: Counting the AB block as only one internal order
corrective_followups: Can A appear before B and B before A inside the block?
How many internal orders are possible?

common_errors.misconception: Arranging five books after treating AB as a block
corrective_followups: How many objects remain when A and B are treated as one block?
Should the block and the other three books be arranged as four objects?

problems.difficulty_rationale: Proves a counting equality by constructing a one-to-one correspondence between strings and position selections.
problems.title: Establish a bijection for binary strings with two ones

student_facing.problem_statement: Prove that the number of binary strings of length 6 containing exactly two 1s is C(6,2). Describe a bijection between the strings and two-element subsets of the six positions.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Each string has six ordered positions, and exactly two positions contain 1. All other positions contain 0.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: There are C(6,2)=15 such strings.
step_by_step_solution: Given a binary string with exactly two 1s, record the set of positions where the 1s occur.
That set is a two-element subset of {1,2,3,4,5,6}.
Conversely, given any two-element subset, place 1s in exactly those positions and 0s elsewhere.
These two constructions undo one another, so they form a bijection.
The number of strings equals the number of two-element subsets: C(6,2)=15.
formulas_definitions_theorems: A bijection proves two finite sets have the same cardinality.
The number of r-element subsets of an n-element set is C(n,r).
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Defines mappings in both directions, shows they are inverse, and computes the common cardinality.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A six-position diagram showing two selected positions is acceptable if the reversible correspondence is explained.

common_errors.misconception: Counting permutations of the two 1s as distinct
corrective_followups: Do the two symbols 1 have separate identities?
Does swapping their labels change the binary string?

common_errors.misconception: Giving a count without explaining the correspondence
corrective_followups: What information uniquely identifies a string with exactly two 1s?
Can every pair of positions produce exactly one such string?

problems.subject: Discrete Mathematics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Adds assigned outcome probabilities in a finite model that is not uniform.
problems.title: Use a nonuniform finite probability model

student_facing.problem_statement: A spinner has four labeled outcomes with probabilities P(1)=0.10, P(2)=0.20, P(3)=0.30, and P(4)=0.40. Find P(X≥3) and P(X∈{2,4}).
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: The four outcomes are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Their probabilities sum to 1.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

step_by_step_solution: For X≥3, the favorable outcomes are 3 and 4.
Add their probabilities: 0.30+0.40=0.70.
For X∈{2,4}, add the probabilities of 2 and 4: 0.20+0.40=0.60.
Check that the four assigned probabilities sum to 1.
formulas_definitions_theorems: For disjoint outcomes, the probability of their union is the sum of their probabilities.
A nonuniform sample space does not use outcome count divided by total count.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Selects the correct outcome sets and adds the assigned probabilities rather than treating the outcomes as equally likely.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A probability bar chart or table is acceptable.

common_errors.misconception: Using 2/4 for an event with two outcomes
corrective_followups: Are the four spinner outcomes equally likely?
What probability is assigned to each favorable outcome?

common_errors.misconception: Multiplying probabilities of mutually exclusive spinner outcomes
corrective_followups: Can two different spinner labels occur on the same spin?
What rule applies to disjoint outcomes?

problems.difficulty_rationale: Finds an event probability by subtracting the complement from one.
problems.title: Apply the complement rule

student_facing.problem_statement: A fair die is rolled once. Find the probability that the result is not 1 or 2. Use the complement rule and verify by listing favorable outcomes.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: The six outcomes are equally likely.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: P(not {1,2})=1−2/6=4/6=2/3; favorable outcomes are {3,4,5,6}.

Direct counting also gives 4/6=2/3.
formulas_definitions_theorems: An event and its complement are disjoint and exhaustive.

instructor_only.alternative_methods: Direct counting alone is acceptable if the complement relationship is also stated.

What is the complement of {1,2}?

corrective_followups: How many outcomes are excluded by “not 1 or 2”?

problems.difficulty_rationale: Multiplies changing conditional probabilities for successive draws without replacement.
problems.title: Calculate a probability without replacement

student_facing.problem_statement: A box contains 5 red cards and 3 blue cards. Two cards are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability that both cards are red. Show the changing denominator.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Each card is equally likely at each draw. The first card is not returned before the second draw.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

step_by_step_solution: The probability the first card is red is 5/8.
After a red card is drawn, 4 red cards remain among 7 total cards.
The conditional probability that the second card is red is 4/7.
formulas_definitions_theorems: P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B|A).
Without replacement, the composition and denominator change after the first draw.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Uses the correct first-draw probability and updates both the red count and total count for the second draw.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A combinations method C(5,2)/C(8,2) is acceptable and gives 10/28=5/14.

common_errors.misconception: Using (5/8)(5/8) as if the first card were replaced
corrective_followups: Does the first red card return to the box?
How many red cards and total cards remain?

common_errors.misconception: Using 4/8 for the second draw
corrective_followups: After one card is removed, how many cards remain in the box?
What is the new denominator?

problems.difficulty_rationale: Counts a union by splitting it into two mutually exclusive event categories.
problems.title: Partition an event into disjoint dice outcomes

student_facing.problem_statement: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. Find the probability that the sum is 7 or the two dice show a double. Show why the two event groups are disjoint.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Ordered outcomes are used, so the sample space has 36 equally likely pairs.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: There are 6 outcomes with sum 7 and 6 doubles; the events are disjoint. Probability=(6+6)/36=1/3.
step_by_step_solution: There are 36 ordered outcomes in total.
No double has sum 7, so the event groups are disjoint.
The union has 12 outcomes, so its probability is 12/36=1/3.
formulas_definitions_theorems: For disjoint events A and B, P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B).
Two ordered fair dice have 6×6=36 equally likely outcomes.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Enumerates both event sets, verifies there is no overlap, and adds their counts over the 36-outcome sample space.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A 6×6 outcome grid is acceptable if the two event groups are marked separately.

corrective_followups: Does any double have a sum of 7?

problems.subject: Discrete Mathematics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Compares probabilities under two different sampling mechanisms and explains how replacement changes dependence.
problems.title: Compare two random-selection mechanisms

student_facing.problem_statement: A container has 2 red and 2 blue tokens. Compare: (A) selecting 2 tokens uniformly without replacement, and (B) drawing twice with replacement. For each mechanism, find the probability that the two selected colors match. Explain why the answers differ.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Every token is equally likely at each draw. In mechanism A, the two selected physical tokens are distinct. In mechanism B, the first token is returned before the second draw.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: Without replacement: P(same color)=2/6=1/3. With replacement: P(same color)=(1/2)(1/2)+(1/2)(1/2)=1/2.
step_by_step_solution: Without replacement, there are C(4,2)=6 unordered token pairs.
Two pairs are same-color: the pair of red tokens and the pair of blue tokens. Thus P(A)=2/6=1/3.
With replacement, P(RR)=1/2·1/2=1/4 and P(BB)=1/2·1/2=1/4.
The same-color probability is 1/4+1/4=1/2.
Without replacement, the first draw changes the composition; with replacement, the original color probabilities are restored.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Without replacement: use combinations or conditional probabilities.
With replacement: successive draws are independent under the stated mechanism.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Models both mechanisms separately, obtains 1/3 and 1/2, and explains the effect of replacement on the second draw.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A tree diagram is acceptable for both mechanisms if branch probabilities are updated correctly.

common_errors.misconception: Using the with-replacement calculation for both mechanisms
corrective_followups: Is the first token returned before the second draw in mechanism A?
What are the second-draw color probabilities after a red token is removed?

common_errors.misconception: Counting RR and BB as equally likely under an unbalanced container
corrective_followups: How many red and blue tokens are present?
Would the calculation change if the initial color counts were unequal?

problems.subject: Discrete Mathematics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Uses exact counting to show that equal-looking categories need not have equal probabilities when their counts differ.
problems.title: Test an apparent symmetry claim in an unequal urn

student_facing.problem_statement: An urn contains 3 red tokens and 2 blue tokens. Two tokens are selected uniformly without replacement. A learner claims that “both red” and “both blue” are equally likely because both events describe matching colors. Compute both probabilities and evaluate the claim.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: All unordered pairs of distinct physical tokens are equally likely.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

step_by_step_solution: There are C(5,2)=10 equally likely token pairs.
There are C(3,2)=3 red-red pairs, so P(RR)=3/10.
There is C(2,2)=1 blue-blue pair, so P(BB)=1/10.
The events are both same-color events, but the numbers of available red and blue pairs differ.
Therefore the stated symmetry claim is false.
formulas_definitions_theorems: For equally likely finite outcomes, event probability is favorable count divided by total count.
The number of same-color pairs from k tokens is C(k,2).
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Counts the sample space and both favorable subsets, then identifies the unequal color counts as the reason the probabilities differ.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A labeled-token list or probability tree is acceptable if it accounts for all ten unordered pairs.

common_errors.misconception: Assigning 1/2 to each event because there are two colors
corrective_followups: Are the two color groups the same size?
How many pairs can be formed within each color?

common_errors.misconception: Using 3/5 and 2/5 as the probabilities of two-token events
corrective_followups: Are you finding a one-draw probability or a two-token pair probability?
How many unordered pairs are in the sample space?

student_facing.problem_statement: Let A={0,1,2,3,4} and define f:A→ℤ by f(x)=x+2. Find the preimage f⁻¹({4}) and state the image f(A).

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Evaluates a removable-form limit by factoring and cancelling a common factor.
problems.title: Evaluate an elementary limit by factoring

student_facing.problem_statement: Evaluate limₓ→2 (x²−4)/(x−2). Show why direct substitution is insufficient and identify the simplified expression near x=2.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: The limit concerns x values near 2 with x≠2. The expression is not defined at x=2 before simplification.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: The limit is 4 because (x²−4)/(x−2)=(x−2)(x+2)/(x−2)=x+2 for x≠2.
step_by_step_solution: Direct substitution gives 0/0, which is indeterminate and does not determine the limit.
Factor the numerator: x²−4=(x−2)(x+2).
For x≠2, cancel the common factor x−2.
The simplified expression near 2 is x+2.
As x approaches 2, x+2 approaches 4.
formulas_definitions_theorems: x²−a²=(x−a)(x+a).
A limit depends on values arbitrarily near the point, not necessarily the function's value at the point.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Recognizes 0/0 as indeterminate, factors correctly, cancels only for x≠2, and evaluates the resulting limit.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A graph or numerical table is acceptable as a check, but the algebraic limit argument is required.

common_errors.misconception: Declaring the limit undefined because the original denominator is zero at 2
corrective_followups: Does a limit require the function to be defined at the point?
Can you simplify the expression for nearby x values?

common_errors.misconception: Cancelling x−2 without factoring the numerator
corrective_followups: What factorization creates a common factor?
Can you rewrite x²−4 as a product?

problems.difficulty_rationale: Applies the power rule term by term to a polynomial.
problems.title: Differentiate a polynomial using the power rule

student_facing.problem_statement: Find f′(x) for f(x)=5x³−2x²+7. Show the derivative of each term.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Differentiate with respect to x. The derivative of a constant is zero.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

step_by_step_solution: For 5x³, multiply by the exponent 3 and reduce the exponent to 2: 15x².
For −2x², multiply by 2 and reduce the exponent to 1: −4x.
The derivative of 7 is 0.
Combine the terms: f′(x)=15x²−4x.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Power rule: d/dx[cxⁿ]=cnxⁿ⁻¹.
d/dx[c]=0 for a constant c.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Applies the power rule to each term, preserves coefficients and signs, and removes the constant term.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A term-by-term derivative table is acceptable.

common_errors.misconception: Keeping the exponent unchanged
corrective_followups: What happens to the exponent under the power rule?
What coefficient is produced by multiplying by the original exponent?

common_errors.misconception: Differentiating 7 as 7x or as 1
corrective_followups: Is 7 a constant term or a variable term?
What is the derivative of a constant?

problems.difficulty_rationale: Integrates a polynomial derivative and uses an initial condition to determine the constant.
problems.title: Recover an antiderivative from an initial value

student_facing.problem_statement: A function f satisfies f′(x)=6x−4 and f(1)=3. Find an explicit formula for f(x). Verify your result by differentiation and substitution.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: f is differentiable on the real numbers. The initial condition is f(1)=3.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

step_by_step_solution: Integrate term by term: f(x)=∫(6x−4)dx=3x²−4x+C.
Solve C=4.
Thus f(x)=3x²−4x+4.
Differentiate to obtain 6x−4 and evaluate f(1)=3.
formulas_definitions_theorems: ∫xⁿdx=xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)+C for n≠−1.
An initial value determines the integration constant.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Finds the general antiderivative, applies the initial condition correctly, and verifies both derivative and function value.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A derivative check followed by solving for C is required; equivalent algebraic forms are acceptable.

common_errors.misconception: Omitting the integration constant
corrective_followups: Can two functions have the same derivative but different constant terms?
What family of antiderivatives corresponds to f′?

common_errors.misconception: Substituting x=1 into f′ instead of f
corrective_followups: Which condition is given: f(1)=3 or f′(1)=3?
Where should the initial value be applied?

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Compares critical points and endpoints on a restricted feasible interval.
problems.title: Optimize a function when the maximum may be at a boundary

student_facing.problem_statement: A rectangular garden uses a wall as one side, so fencing is needed for the other three sides. Let x be the width and let the fenced length be 20−2x metres. A site rule restricts 0≤x≤4. Maximize A(x)=x(20−2x) on this interval and state the dimensions.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: The area function is defined on the closed feasible interval [0,4]. Width and length must be nonnegative.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: A′(x)=20−4x>0 on [0,4], so the maximum occurs at the boundary x=4. Length=12 m; maximum area=48 m².
step_by_step_solution: Expand A(x)=20x−2x².
Differentiate: A′(x)=20−4x.
For 0≤x≤4, A′(x)≥4>0, so A is increasing throughout the feasible interval.
Therefore the maximum occurs at the right endpoint x=4.
Length=20−2(4)=12 m and area=4·12=48 m².
Check the endpoints: A(0)=0 and A(4)=48.
formulas_definitions_theorems: For a continuous function on a closed interval, absolute extrema occur at critical points or endpoints.
A′(x)>0 throughout an interval implies A is increasing there.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Uses the domain restriction, checks derivative sign on the feasible interval, and selects the boundary maximum rather than an infeasible critical point.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A complete endpoint/critical-point table is acceptable.

common_errors.misconception: Using the unconstrained critical point x=5
corrective_followups: Is x=5 allowed by the site restriction?
Which points are feasible in [0,4]?

common_errors.misconception: Checking only where A′(x)=0
corrective_followups: Can a maximum occur at an endpoint of a closed interval?
Have you compared the feasible endpoints?

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Integrates domain, asymptote, intercept, and monotonicity analysis for a rational function.
problems.title: Analyze a rational function with a vertical asymptote

student_facing.problem_statement: Analyze f(x)=(x+1)/(x−2). State its domain, vertical and horizontal asymptotes, x- and y-intercepts, and intervals of increase or decrease. Justify each result.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: The function is considered over real x where the denominator is nonzero.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: Domain ℝ\{2}; vertical asymptote x=2; horizontal asymptote y=1; x-intercept (−1,0); y-intercept (0,−1/2); f′(x)=−3/(x−2)²<0, so it decreases on (−∞,2) and (2,∞).
step_by_step_solution: The denominator is zero at x=2, so exclude 2 from the domain.
As x approaches 2, the denominator approaches zero while the numerator approaches 3, giving a vertical asymptote x=2.
The numerator and denominator have equal degree and leading-coefficient ratio 1, so the horizontal asymptote is y=1.
Set the numerator equal to zero: x=−1, giving (−1,0).
Differentiate by the quotient rule: f′(x)=[(x−2)−(x+1)]/(x−2)²=−3/(x−2)².
The derivative is negative on both domain intervals, so f decreases on each interval.
formulas_definitions_theorems: For f(x)=P(x)/Q(x), zeros of Q are excluded from the domain.
For equal numerator and denominator degrees, the horizontal asymptote is the ratio of leading coefficients.
Quotient rule: (u/v)′=(u′v−uv′)/v².
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Derives the domain and asymptotes from the formula, calculates both intercepts, and uses the derivative sign on each connected domain interval.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: Algebraic rewriting f(x)=1+3/(x−2) is acceptable for identifying asymptotes, followed by derivative analysis.

common_errors.misconception: Calling y=2 the horizontal asymptote because the denominator contains x−2
corrective_followups: What happens to the ratio as x becomes very large in magnitude?
What is the ratio of the leading coefficients?

common_errors.misconception: Claiming the function increases because the numerator increases
corrective_followups: What does the derivative say about the rate of change?
Is f′ positive or negative on either side of x=2?

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Derives a piecewise optimum as a parameter changes the feasible interval.
problems.title: Optimize a parameterized function with a restricted domain

student_facing.problem_statement: For a parameter a≥0, maximize A(x)=x(12−x) subject to 0≤x≤a. Find the maximizing x and maximum value A_max(a) as piecewise expressions. Explain what changes when a passes 6.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: The feasible interval is [0,a]. The objective is a concave quadratic and x represents a nonnegative design variable.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: x*=a and A_max= a(12−a) for 0≤a≤6; x*=6 and A_max=36 for a≥6.
step_by_step_solution: Differentiate: A′(x)=12−2x; the unconstrained critical point is x=6.
The second derivative is A″(x)=−2<0, so the objective is concave and x=6 is its unconstrained maximum.
If 0≤a≤6, the feasible interval ends at or before 6 and A increases throughout [0,a]; the maximum is x=a.
If a≥6, the feasible interval contains x=6, so the maximum is attained at x=6.
Thus A_max(a)=a(12−a) for 0≤a≤6 and 36 for a≥6.
At a=6, both expressions give 36, so the pieces join continuously.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Critical point: A′(x)=0.
A″(x)<0 establishes concavity.
A constrained maximum must lie in the feasible interval.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Finds the unconstrained critical point, compares it with the parameterized feasible boundary, and states the correct piecewise solution.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A graph showing the moving endpoint a relative to the vertex x=6 is acceptable as a supporting explanation.

common_errors.misconception: Using x=6 even when a<6
corrective_followups: Is x=6 feasible when the allowed interval ends before 6?
Where does the increasing function reach its maximum on [0,a]?

common_errors.misconception: Using x=a for all a, including a>6
corrective_followups: Does the function continue increasing after x=6?
What does the derivative sign show beyond the critical point?

problems.difficulty_rationale: Extracts frequency, relative frequency, and mode from a small frequency table.
problems.title: Read a frequency table

student_facing.problem_statement: A class records daily study hours for six learners: 1 hour occurs 2 times, 2 hours occurs 3 times, and 3 hours occurs 1 time. Find the total frequency, the relative frequency for 2 hours, and the mode.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: The frequency table is complete and each learner contributes one observation.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: Total frequency=6; relative frequency at 2 hours=3/6=0.50; mode=2 hours.
step_by_step_solution: Add frequencies: 2+3+1=6.
Divide the frequency for 2 hours by the total: 3/6=0.50 or 50%.
The highest frequency is 3, associated with 2 hours, so the mode is 2 hours.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Relative frequency=f/ n.
The mode is the observed value with the greatest frequency.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Adds all frequencies, calculates the specified relative frequency using the total, and identifies the value with the largest frequency.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A reconstructed six-row data list is acceptable.

problems.title: Find the median from an even-sized data set

student_facing.problem_statement: The ordered waiting times, in minutes, are 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, and 12. Find the median and explain why two values are averaged.

The third and fourth values are 7 and 8.

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Computes and interprets the range as a difference in the original measurement unit.
problems.title: Interpret a range with measurement units

student_facing.problem_statement: Four afternoon temperatures are 18°C, 21°C, 24°C, and 29°C. Find the range and explain what the result says about the spread of these observations.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: The values are measurements on the Celsius scale. Range is maximum minus minimum.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: Range=29−18=11°C; the highest observation is 11°C above the lowest.
step_by_step_solution: Identify the maximum: 29°C.
Identify the minimum: 18°C.
Subtract: 29−18=11.
Report 11°C and interpret it as the distance between the extreme observations.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Range=max−min.
A difference in Celsius measurements is expressed in degrees Celsius.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Identifies the extreme values, subtracts minimum from maximum, and interprets the range without calling it an average.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A sorted list is acceptable if the endpoints and difference are clear.

common_errors.misconception: Subtracting maximum from minimum and reporting a negative range
corrective_followups: Which value is the maximum?
How is range conventionally defined?

common_errors.misconception: Calling 11°C the average temperature
corrective_followups: Does range describe a center or the distance between extremes?
What information does the range omit?

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Applies a stated median-of-halves convention and uses IQR fences to flag a potential outlier.
problems.title: Calculate quartiles and identify an outlier

student_facing.problem_statement: For the ordered data 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 20, use the median-of-halves convention to find Q1, Q3, the interquartile range, and the 1.5×IQR outlier fences. Is 20 flagged as an outlier?
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: The data are ordered. For eight observations, split into the lower four and upper four; each quartile is the median of its half.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: Q1=3.5; Q3=7.5; IQR=4; lower fence=−2.5; upper fence=13.5; 20 is flagged as an outlier.
step_by_step_solution: Lower fence=Q1−1.5(IQR)=3.5−6=−2.5.
Upper fence=Q3+1.5(IQR)=7.5+6=13.5.
Since 20>13.5, it is flagged as a potential outlier.
formulas_definitions_theorems: IQR=Q3−Q1.
Potential outlier fences are Q1−1.5(IQR) and Q3+1.5(IQR).
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Uses the specified quartile convention, calculates IQR and both fences, and compares 20 with the upper fence.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A boxplot calculation is acceptable if the quartile convention is stated.

common_errors.misconception: Using 20 as part of the lower half
corrective_followups: Where is the median split for eight ordered values?
Which four observations form the upper half?

common_errors.misconception: Calling every value above Q3 an outlier
corrective_followups: What is the actual upper fence?
Does 20 exceed Q3 or the more distant 1.5×IQR fence?

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Identifies volunteer-response bias and proposes a probability sampling alternative.
problems.title: Compare volunteer and probability sampling

student_facing.problem_statement: A university wants to estimate the average weekly study time of all first-year students. It posts an optional online survey and uses the first 200 responses. Identify the sampling method and one likely source of bias. Propose a more defensible sampling design.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: The target population is all first-year students. Participation in the posted survey is voluntary.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: The method is a voluntary-response sample. It may overrepresent students with strong opinions, high internet engagement, or more available time. A simple random sample or a stratified random sample by program/section is more defensible.
step_by_step_solution: The sample consists of people who choose to respond, so it is a voluntary-response sample.
Students who notice the post and decide to respond may differ from nonrespondents.
This creates self-selection/voluntary-response bias and may reduce representativeness.
Construct a sampling frame of first-year students and select a random sample.
If programs or sections differ, stratify by those groups and randomly sample within each stratum.
formulas_definitions_theorems: A probability sample gives population members known, nonzero selection chances.
Stratified sampling samples randomly within defined population subgroups.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Names the sampling mechanism, explains a plausible selection bias, and proposes a probability-based design tied to the target population.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: Cluster or systematic sampling can be acceptable if the frame, selection process, and limitations are justified.

common_errors.misconception: Calling the sample a simple random sample because 200 people responded
corrective_followups: Did the researcher randomly select the 200 students?
Who decided whether to participate?

common_errors.misconception: Claiming a larger volunteer sample removes selection bias
corrective_followups: Would increasing the number of volunteers guarantee representation?
How could random selection reduce self-selection effects?

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Computes population central moments under an explicit convention and interprets standardized skewness.
problems.title: Audit a standardized third-moment calculation

student_facing.problem_statement: Treat the data 1, 1, 2, 4 as the complete population. Compute the mean, second central moment μ₂, third central moment μ₃, and moment coefficient of skewness γ₁=μ₃/(μ₂)^(3/2). Interpret the sign and approximate magnitude.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Use population moments with denominator n=4. Do not apply a sample bias correction.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: Mean=2; μ₂=1.5; μ₃=1.5; γ₁=1.5/(1.5)^(3/2)=√(2/3)≈0.8165. The distribution is positively skewed.
step_by_step_solution: Deviations from the mean are −1,−1,0,2.
The squared deviations sum to 1+1+0+4=6, so μ₂=6/4=1.5.
The cubed deviations sum to −1−1+0+8=6, so μ₃=6/4=1.5.
The positive value indicates a longer/right-side tail in the direction of larger observations.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Population central moment μ_r=(1/n)Σ(x_i−μ)^r.
Moment skewness γ₁=μ₃/(μ₂)^(3/2).
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: States the population convention, calculates both central moments correctly, standardizes the third moment, and interprets its positive sign.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A calculator result is acceptable if the deviations, moment convention, and formula are shown.

common_errors.misconception: Using n−1 for the population central moments
corrective_followups: Does the problem treat these four values as a sample or the complete population?
Which denominator is specified?

common_errors.misconception: Interpreting positive skewness as a longer left tail
corrective_followups: Which side contains the more extreme large observation?

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Derives how translation and positive scaling affect center and spread measures.
problems.title: Analyze how a linear transformation changes variability

student_facing.problem_statement: Let X have population values {2,4,6}, and define Y=3X+5 for each observation. Find the means, ranges, population variances, and population standard deviations of X and Y. State which measures change under adding 5 and multiplying by 3.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Use population variance with denominator n=3. Apply the transformation to every observation.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: Y={11,17,23}; means 4 and 17; ranges 4 and 12; variances 8/3 and 24; standard deviations √(8/3) and √24=3√(8/3).
step_by_step_solution: For X, mean=(2+4+6)/3=4; deviations are −2,0,2.
Population variance of X is (4+0+4)/3=8/3; SD is √(8/3); range is 6−2=4.
Transform values: Y={11,17,23}; mean=17; range=23−11=12.
Y deviations from 17 are −6,0,6; variance=(36+0+36)/3=24; SD=√24.
Adding 5 shifts the mean but does not change spread; multiplying by 3 multiplies range and SD by 3 and variance by 9.
formulas_definitions_theorems: For Y=aX+b: mean(Y)=a·mean(X)+b.
Var(aX+b)=a²Var(X); SD(aX+b)=|a|SD(X); range(aX+b)=|a|range(X).
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Computes both data sets and identifies the separate effects of translation and scaling on center and variability.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: Using the transformation formulas directly is acceptable if the original and transformed statistics are shown.

common_errors.misconception: Adding 5 to the variance
corrective_followups: Does shifting every observation change its distance from the mean?
Which transformation component changes the spread?

common_errors.misconception: Multiplying variance by 3 instead of 9
corrective_followups: Variance uses squared deviations. What happens when every deviation is multiplied by 3?
What is 3²?

problems.difficulty_rationale: Uses the addition rule for two events that cannot occur together.

student_facing.problem_statement: Among 30 participants, 18 use a study app, 12 completed a practice task, and 9 both use the app and completed the task. Find the probability that a participant completed the task given that the participant uses the app.

The overlap count is 9 and the app-user count is 18.

The denominator is the size/probability of the conditioned group.

student_facing.problem_statement: A survey of 50 learners records study time and task completion. There are 30 morning learners and 20 evening learners. Of the morning learners, 18 passed; of the evening learners, 6 passed. Find P(pass|morning) and P(pass). Are passing and being a morning learner independent?
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Each learner belongs to exactly one study-time group. There are 24 passes in total.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: P(pass|morning)=18/30=0.60; P(pass)=24/50=0.48. They are not independent because the conditional and marginal probabilities differ.
step_by_step_solution: Morning passes=18 and evening passes=6, so total passes=24.
P(pass|morning)=18/30=0.60.
Independence would require P(pass|morning)=P(pass), assuming P(morning)>0.
Since 0.60≠0.48, the events are not independent.
formulas_definitions_theorems: A and B are independent iff P(A|B)=P(A) when P(B)>0.

instructor_only.alternative_methods: Checking P(pass∩morning)=P(pass)P(morning) is also acceptable: 18/50≠(24/50)(30/50).

An intersection contains outcomes satisfying both event conditions.

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Combines three source proportions and source-specific defect rates to calculate posterior source probabilities.
problems.title: Use Bayes' theorem with three suppliers

student_facing.problem_statement: A factory receives 50% of its parts from supplier A, 30% from B, and 20% from C. Their defect rates are 1%, 2%, and 5%, respectively. A randomly selected part is defective. Find the probability it came from supplier C. Show the total-probability denominator.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Each part comes from exactly one supplier. The stated defect rates are conditional on supplier source.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

step_by_step_solution: Compute the joint contribution from A: 0.50·0.01=0.005.
Compute the contribution from B: 0.30·0.02=0.006.
Compute the contribution from C: 0.20·0.05=0.010.
Total defect probability is 0.005+0.006+0.010=0.021.
Bayes' theorem gives P(C|D)=0.010/0.021=10/21≈0.4762.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Total probability: P(D)=ΣᵢP(D|Sᵢ)P(Sᵢ).
Bayes: P(C|D)=P(D|C)P(C)/P(D).
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Uses source proportions as priors, computes each source's defect contribution, forms the total defect probability, and applies Bayes' theorem.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A probability tree is acceptable if branch probabilities and joint paths are multiplied and normalized correctly.

common_errors.misconception: Using 5% directly as P(C|D)
corrective_followups: Is 5% the defect rate among C parts or the probability a defective part came from C?
What prior share of parts comes from C?

common_errors.misconception: Dividing the C contribution by only the A and B contributions
corrective_followups: Does the denominator include every possible supplier source?
What is the total probability of a defective part?

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Derives posterior probability as a function of prevalence and identifies a decision threshold.
problems.title: Analyze posterior probability as the prior changes

student_facing.problem_statement: A screening test has sensitivity 0.90 and false-positive rate 0.10. Let p be disease prevalence. (a) Derive P(disease|positive) as a function of p. (b) Evaluate it for p=0.01 and p=0.10. (c) Find the prevalence at which a positive result is at least 50% likely to indicate disease.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Sensitivity=P(+|D)=0.90; false-positive rate=P(+|not D)=0.10. The population is partitioned into diseased and non-diseased people.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

step_by_step_solution: Apply Bayes' theorem with P(D)=p and P(not D)=1−p.
Simplify the denominator: 0.9p+0.1−0.1p=0.1+0.8p.
For posterior at least 0.5, solve 0.9p≥0.1(1−p), giving p≥0.10.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Bayes' theorem for a positive test.
Posterior probability depends on both test characteristics and prior prevalence.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Derives the posterior function, evaluates both prevalences accurately, and solves the threshold inequality with the correct prior interpretation.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A probability tree or algebraic inequality is acceptable if it produces the same posterior and threshold.

common_errors.misconception: Claiming a 90% positive result means a 90% chance of disease
corrective_followups: What does sensitivity condition on?
What additional probability is needed to reverse the condition?

common_errors.misconception: Using p as the false-positive rate
corrective_followups: Which symbol represents prevalence and which represents P(+|not D)?
Can you label the prior and likelihood separately?

problems.difficulty_rationale: Identifies the four conditions required for a binomial random variable.

student_facing.problem_statement: A quality inspector checks 8 independently selected items. Each item has a 0.20 probability of being defective, and the item is classified as defective or not defective. Let X be the number of defective items. State the distribution of X and its parameters, and identify the binomial conditions.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: The sample size is fixed at 8. The defect probability is constant and item outcomes are independent.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: X~Binomial(n=8,p=0.20).
step_by_step_solution: There is a fixed number of trials: n=8.
Each trial has two categories: defective or not defective.

student_facing.problem_statement: Let X be uniformly distributed on [0,10]. Find P(X=4) and P(3<X<5). Explain why the two answers differ.

student_facing.problem_statement: A shipment contains 12 components, of which 4 are defective and 8 are good. An inspector selects 3 components without replacement. Find the probability that exactly one selected component is defective.

step_by_step_solution: Choose 1 defective from 4: C(4,1)=4.

Sampling without replacement from a finite population with fixed category counts is hypergeometric.

problems.difficulty_rationale: Converts a standard-normal percentile into the original measurement scale.
problems.title: Find a normal-distribution percentile

student_facing.problem_statement: A measurement X is normally distributed with mean 70 and standard deviation 10. The 84.13th percentile of the standard normal distribution is approximately z=1.00. Estimate the 84.13th percentile of X.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: X~N(70,10²). Use the supplied standard-normal percentile z=1.00.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

step_by_step_solution: Use the standardization relation z=(x−μ)/σ.
Rearrange to x=μ+zσ.
Substitute μ=70, σ=10, and z=1.00.
formulas_definitions_theorems: z=(x−μ)/σ.
The percentile on the original scale is x=μ+zσ.

instructor_only.alternative_methods: A normal-curve sketch is acceptable as a check.

corrective_followups: Which quantity measures the scale of deviations from the mean?

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Calculates a multinomial count probability and explains dependence created by a fixed total.
problems.title: Analyze multinomial category counts and dependence

student_facing.problem_statement: Each of 5 independent trials results in category A, B, or C with probabilities 0.50, 0.30, and 0.20. Let N_A,N_B,N_C be the category counts. Find P(N_A=2,N_B=2,N_C=1). Then compute Cov(N_A,N_B) and explain why the counts are not independent.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Trials are independent and each trial has exactly one of the three categories. The total count is fixed at 5.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

step_by_step_solution: There are 5!/(2!2!1!)=30 arrangements of the category labels with the requested counts.
Each such arrangement has probability (0.5)²(0.3)²(0.2).
For multinomial counts, Cov(N_A,N_B)=−np_Ap_B for distinct categories.
The counts share a fixed total; an increase in one category leaves fewer trials available for the others, producing negative dependence.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Multinomial probability: n!/(n₁!…n_k!)∏pᵢⁿⁱ.
For i≠j, Cov(Nᵢ,Nⱼ)=−npᵢpⱼ.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Uses the multinomial coefficient and category probabilities correctly, calculates covariance, and explains the fixed-total dependence.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A sequential tree calculation over all category orders is acceptable if it accounts for all 30 arrangements.

common_errors.misconception: Using a product of binomial probabilities as if category counts were independent
corrective_followups: Do the three category counts vary independently when their sum must equal 5?
What constraint links N_A, N_B, and N_C?

common_errors.misconception: Omitting the multinomial coefficient
corrective_followups: How many distinct orderings produce the same count vector?
What does the factorial ratio count?

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Compares an exact binomial probability with a Poisson approximation and evaluates a stated tolerance.
problems.title: Evaluate an exact-versus-Poisson approximation

student_facing.problem_statement: A batch has 20 independent items, each defective with probability 0.03. Let X be the number of defective items. Compare the exact binomial value of P(X=0) with the Poisson approximation using λ=np. Is the absolute error below 0.01? Explain why the approximation is reasonable or not.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: The number of trials is fixed at n=20 and each item has the same independent defect probability p=0.03.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: Exact: P(X=0)=0.97²⁰≈0.54379. Poisson λ=0.6 gives e^(−0.6)≈0.54881. Absolute error≈0.00502, which is below 0.01.
step_by_step_solution: The exact model is X~Binomial(20,0.03).
The Poisson approximation uses λ=np=20·0.03=0.6.
Since 0.005018<0.01, the stated tolerance is met. The approximation is plausible because n is moderate and p is small, though exact binomial remains available.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Binomial zero-count probability: (1−p)^n.
Poisson approximation parameter: λ=np.
Poisson zero-count probability: e^(−λ).
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Identifies the exact binomial model, computes λ, compares both probabilities, and tests the numerical error against the specified tolerance.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A calculator or script may be used for exponentiation if the formulas and comparison are shown.

corrective_followups: What is the expected number of defects across 20 items?

corrective_followups: What numerical tolerance is specified?

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Eliminates alternatives that violate mandatory constraints before comparing feasible options.
problems.title: Apply a feasibility screen before scoring

student_facing.problem_statement: A department needs a laptop costing no more than ₱20,000 with battery life of at least 8 hours. Four options are: A ₱18,000 and 7 hours; B ₱21,000 and 10 hours; C ₱19,000 and 9 hours; D ₱17,000 and 8 hours. Identify the feasible options and explain why the other options must be rejected before weighted scoring.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Both requirements are mandatory: price≤₱20,000 and battery life≥8 hours. Meeting one cannot compensate for violating the other.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: Options C and D are feasible. A fails the battery requirement; B fails the price requirement.
step_by_step_solution: Test A: price passes, battery 7<8 fails.
Test B: battery passes, price ₱21,000>₱20,000 fails.
Test C: price and battery both pass.
Test D: price and battery both pass, with battery exactly at the minimum.
Retain C and D for later preference scoring; exclude A and B as infeasible.
formulas_definitions_theorems: A feasible alternative satisfies every mandatory constraint.
Feasibility screening should precede compensatory weighted scoring when constraints are non-negotiable.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Applies both constraints to every option, treats equality at the minimum as acceptable, and distinguishes mandatory feasibility from preference scoring.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A pass/fail constraint matrix is acceptable.

common_errors.misconception: Accepting B because its battery life is excellent
corrective_followups: Can a high score on one criterion override a mandatory budget limit?
Which conditions must every feasible option satisfy?

common_errors.misconception: Rejecting D because its battery is exactly 8 hours
corrective_followups: Does “at least 8” include equality?

problems.difficulty_rationale: Computes weighted scores and interprets a result without treating weights as objective facts.
problems.title: Evaluate alternatives with a weighted decision matrix

student_facing.problem_statement: A committee rates two scheduling systems from 1 to 10. Weights are reliability 0.50, ease of use 0.30, and cost suitability 0.20. System P scores 8, 7, 6; System Q scores 7, 9, 8. Compute each weighted score and identify the higher-scoring system. State one limitation of the result.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: All criteria use the same 1–10 scale and higher ratings are preferred. The supplied weights sum to 1.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

step_by_step_solution: Multiply each rating by its criterion weight.
Compare the totals: Q is higher by 0.5 points.
The ranking depends on the chosen weights and ratings; it does not prove Q is objectively best.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Weighted score S=Σwᵢrᵢ, where weights sum to 1.
A weighted matrix is compensatory unless mandatory constraints are applied separately.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Multiplies each rating by the correct weight, sums the contributions, and notes that scores depend on subjective ratings and weight choices.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A spreadsheet-style weighted table is acceptable.

common_errors.misconception: Adding raw ratings without applying weights
corrective_followups: Are all criteria equally important under the supplied weights?
How should each rating be scaled?

common_errors.misconception: Treating the highest weighted score as an objective truth
corrective_followups: Who selected the weights and ratings?
How might a different priority change the ranking?

problems.difficulty_rationale: Derives a break-even weight and determines whether a recommendation is robust over an allowed weight range.
problems.title: Test sensitivity to uncertain criterion weights

student_facing.problem_statement: Two alternatives are rated on cost suitability and reliability. Alternative A scores 9 on cost and 6 on reliability. Alternative B scores 7 on cost and 9 on reliability. Let w be the weight on reliability, so cost has weight 1−w. Analyze the preferred alternative for 0.40≤w≤0.60. Identify the break-even weight.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Ratings are fixed. Weights are nonnegative and sum to 1. Higher weighted score is preferred.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: S_A=9(1−w)+6w=9−3w. S_B=7(1−w)+9w=7+2w. They tie at w=0.40; B is higher for w>0.40. Across [0.40,0.60], B is never worse and is strictly preferred above 0.40.
step_by_step_solution: Write A's score: S_A=9(1−w)+6w=9−3w.
Write B's score: S_B=7(1−w)+9w=7+2w.
Set the scores equal: 9−3w=7+2w.
Solve 2=5w, so w=0.40.
For w>0.40, S_B−S_A=5w−2>0, so B wins; at w=0.40 they tie.
Within the allowed interval, B is not worse anywhere and is better except at the lower endpoint.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Weighted score S=(1−w)(cost rating)+w(reliability rating).
A break-even weight occurs where competing weighted scores are equal.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Defines the weight variable, derives both score functions, solves the tie point, and interprets the full specified range.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A graph of the two score lines is acceptable if the intersection and preferred region are identified.

corrective_followups: Which criterion is assigned w in the problem?

corrective_followups: How does increasing w affect each alternative's score?

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Separates mandatory eligibility from compensatory preference scoring.
problems.title: Critique a compensatory model with mandatory requirements

student_facing.problem_statement: A scholarship committee must require applicants to meet both a minimum GPA of 3.0 and a completed service requirement. Applicant A has GPA 3.8, strong interview and excellent recommendations but has not completed the service requirement. Applicant B has GPA 3.2 and meets the service requirement. Explain why a weighted score that ranks A first may be invalid, and propose a defensible decision procedure.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: The service requirement and minimum GPA are mandatory eligibility conditions, not preferences.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: Applicant A is ineligible despite strong scores on other criteria. Applicant B is eligible. Apply the mandatory screen first, then score only eligible applicants on preference criteria.
step_by_step_solution: Identify the two noncompensable requirements: GPA≥3.0 and completed service.
Applicant A meets the GPA condition but fails service, so A is infeasible.
Applicant B meets both mandatory conditions, so B remains eligible.
A compensatory weighted sum could let high interview/recommendation ratings offset the failed service condition, contradicting the policy.
First filter applicants by mandatory eligibility; then apply the approved weighted model among those who pass.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Feasibility constraints are noncompensable when policy states they are mandatory.
Weighted-sum models allow trade-offs and should not override hard eligibility rules.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Identifies the mandatory constraints, screens each applicant, explains the compensatory-model failure, and proposes a two-stage procedure.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A lexicographic or constrained optimization model is acceptable if mandatory conditions cannot be traded away.

common_errors.misconception: Selecting A because the weighted total is highest
corrective_followups: Can preference points compensate for failure of a mandatory condition?
Should eligibility be checked before or after scoring?

common_errors.misconception: Rejecting both applicants because A fails one condition
corrective_followups: Does B satisfy both stated requirements?
Which applicant remains in the feasible set?

problems.difficulty_rationale: Interprets conditional branches and calculates a joint path probability.

student_facing.problem_statement: A demand forecast has two possible signals: positive with probability 0.40 and negative with probability 0.60. Given a positive signal, high demand has probability 0.75. Given a negative signal, high demand has probability 0.20. Find the probability of (a) a positive signal and high demand and (b) high demand overall.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: The signal branches are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Conditional probabilities are read within their stated signal branch.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

step_by_step_solution: Multiply along the positive/high path: 0.40·0.75=0.30.
For a negative signal and high demand, multiply 0.60·0.20=0.12.
High demand can occur after either signal, so add the disjoint path probabilities: 0.30+0.12=0.42.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Joint path probability is the product of branch probabilities along a path.
Total probability adds the probabilities of disjoint paths leading to the same event.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Reads each conditional probability from the correct branch, multiplies along paths, and adds the disjoint high-demand paths.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A probability tree with joint path labels is acceptable.

common_errors.misconception: Adding 0.40 and 0.75 for the positive/high path
corrective_followups: Are the signal and demand probabilities on successive branches?
What operation gives the probability of both events along one path?

common_errors.misconception: Using only the positive/high path for total high demand
corrective_followups: Can high demand also occur after a negative signal?
Which disjoint paths lead to high demand?

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Compares a probability-based criterion with a worst-case regret criterion and explains why they may disagree.
problems.title: Compare expected value with minimax regret

student_facing.problem_statement: Two plans have the following payoffs: Plan A earns 100 in high demand and 20 in low demand; Plan B earns 70 in high demand and 60 in low demand. P(high)=0.60 and P(low)=0.40. (a) Choose by expected value. (b) Choose by minimax regret. Explain any difference.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Payoffs are in the same units. Regret in each state is the best payoff in that state minus the payoff of the selected plan.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: EV(A)=68; EV(B)=66, so expected value selects A. Regrets: A=(0,40), maximum 40; B=(30,0), maximum 30, so minimax regret selects B.
step_by_step_solution: Expected value: B=0.60(70)+0.40(60)=66. Thus A is selected by expected value.
For high demand, best payoff is 100: regret A=0, B=30.
For low demand, best payoff is 60: regret A=40, B=0.
Maximum regret is 40 for A and 30 for B.
Minimax regret selects B because its worst regret is smaller.
formulas_definitions_theorems: EV(a)=Σp(s)u(a,s).
Regret(a,s)=best payoff in state s−payoff(a,s).
Minimax regret minimizes the maximum statewise regret.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Computes expected values, constructs statewise regrets from the best payoff in each state, and distinguishes the two decision criteria.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A complete payoff and regret matrix is acceptable.

common_errors.misconception: Calculating regret against the best overall payoff rather than the best in each state
corrective_followups: Which plan has the highest payoff in high demand?
Which plan has the highest payoff in low demand?

common_errors.misconception: Assuming the two criteria must select the same plan
corrective_followups: Does minimax regret use the state probabilities?
What objective does each criterion minimize or maximize?

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Uses signal-specific conditional probabilities to choose an action after observing a forecast.
problems.title: Use a simple signal tree to revise a decision

student_facing.problem_statement: A shop chooses between a high-stock and low-stock plan. High demand pays 100 under high stock and −40 under low demand; low stock pays 50 under high demand and 30 under low demand. A forecast is high or low with equal probability 0.50. Given a high forecast, P(high demand)=0.70; given a low forecast, P(high demand)=0.10. Find the best action after each signal and the expected payoff when the signal is used. Compare with the best expected payoff without the signal.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Forecast branches are mutually exclusive. The stated conditional probabilities are calibrated so P(high demand)=0.50(0.70)+0.50(0.10)=0.40.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: After high signal: high stock EV=58, low stock EV=44, choose high stock. After low signal: high stock EV=−26, low stock EV=32, choose low stock. With signal EV=0.50(58)+0.50(32)=45. Without signal, high stock EV=16 and low stock EV=38, so choose low stock; signal improves expected payoff by 7.
step_by_step_solution: After a high signal, calculate high stock: 0.70(100)+0.30(−40)=58.
After a high signal, low stock gives 0.70(50)+0.30(30)=44; choose high stock.
After a low signal, high stock gives 0.10(100)+0.90(−40)=−26.
After a low signal, low stock gives 0.10(50)+0.90(30)=32; choose low stock.
Expected payoff with signal is 0.50(58)+0.50(32)=45.
Without signal, P(high demand)=0.40. High stock EV=0.40(100)+0.60(−40)=16; low stock EV=0.40(50)+0.60(30)=38.
Without signal choose low stock at 38. The signal increases expected payoff by 45−38=7.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Conditional expected payoff after signal s: ΣP(state|s)·payoff(action,state).
Expected value with sample information averages the best conditional decision over signal outcomes.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Calculates each action's conditional expected payoff for each signal, chooses the best action separately, and compares the resulting expected value with the no-signal decision.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A labeled decision tree or a conditional payoff table is acceptable.

common_errors.misconception: Choosing one action before considering which signal appears
corrective_followups: Can the action be selected after observing the forecast?
What is the best action on each separate signal branch?

common_errors.misconception: Using P(high demand)=0.70 as the unconditional probability
corrective_followups: Is 0.70 conditional on a high forecast?
How do you combine both forecast branches to get the prior probability?

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Calculates the expected value of sample information and converts it into a maximum justifiable information cost.
problems.title: Find the maximum price worth paying for sample information

student_facing.problem_statement: A company must choose whether to launch a product. If demand is high, launch earns 100; if demand is low, launch loses 50. Not launching earns 0 in either state. Prior probabilities are P(high)=0.40 and P(low)=0.60. A market signal has P(+)=0.50, P(−)=0.50, P(high|+)=0.70, and P(high|−)=0.10. Find the best expected payoff without the signal, the expected payoff with the signal before its cost, the expected value of sample information (EVSI), and the maximum price the company should pay for the signal.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: The signal probabilities and conditional demand probabilities are given. The signal cost is paid regardless of which signal occurs.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: Without signal: launch EV=0.40(100)+0.60(−50)=10, so choose launch. With signal: after +, launch EV=55 and is chosen; after −, launch EV=−35, so do not launch. EV with signal=0.50(55)+0.50(0)=27.5. EVSI=27.5−10=17.5. Maximum price=17.5.
step_by_step_solution: Without signal, launch has expected value 40−30=10; not launching has 0, so launch is selected.
After a positive signal, launch EV=0.70(100)+0.30(−50)=55; choose launch.
After a negative signal, launch EV=0.10(100)+0.90(−50)=−35; choose not to launch at 0.
Expected value with signal before cost is 0.50(55)+0.50(0)=27.5.
The company should pay at most 17.5 (in the same payoff units) for the signal; at a higher price the information's net expected value becomes negative.
formulas_definitions_theorems: EVSI=EV with sample information before cost−EV without sample information.
Maximum justifiable information cost equals EVSI when the information is optional and risk-neutral expected value is the criterion.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Optimizes the action before and after the signal, averages the branch-specific optimal payoffs, subtracts the no-information benchmark, and interprets EVSI as a price ceiling.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A decision tree is acceptable if it shows the decision node after each signal and averages the best branch payoffs.

common_errors.misconception: Paying the EVSI in addition to a separate cost without subtracting it
corrective_followups: Is EVSI the value before or after paying for the signal?
What happens to net value when the signal costs exactly 17.5?

common_errors.misconception: Launching after both positive and negative signals
corrective_followups: What is the expected payoff of launch after a negative signal?
Can the decision maker choose not to launch after observing the signal?

problems.subject: Quantitative Methods with Probability and Statistics
problems.difficulty_rationale: Audits posterior branch probabilities, conditional action payoffs, and the net value of a costly imperfect test.
problems.title: Audit a decision tree with a costly imperfect test

student_facing.problem_statement: A unit is defective with prior probability 0.20. An inspection test has sensitivity 0.90 and false-positive rate 0.10. The test costs 2 units. After testing, the manager may replace the unit or keep it. Replacing yields +40 if defective and −20 if not defective; keeping yields −100 if defective and 0 if not defective. (a) Find P(positive) and P(defective|positive). (b) Find P(defective|negative). (c) Determine the best action after each signal. (d) Decide whether testing is worthwhile compared with acting without a test.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Sensitivity=P(+|D)=0.90; false-positive rate=P(+|not D)=0.10; P(D)=0.20. Test cost is incurred for every inspected unit.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: P(+)=0.26; P(D|+)=9/13≈0.6923; P(−)=0.74; P(D|−)=1/37≈0.0270. Without test, replace EV=−8 and keep EV=−20, so replace. After +, replace EV=280/13≈21.538. After −, keep EV=−100/37≈−2.703, better than replacing. Expected payoff with test before cost=3.6; after cost=1.6. Testing is worthwhile because 1.6>−8.
step_by_step_solution: Without a test: replace EV=0.20(40)+0.80(−20)=−8; keep EV=0.20(−100)+0.80(0)=−20. Choose replace at −8.
After a positive test: replace EV=(9/13)(40)+(4/13)(−20)=280/13≈21.538; keeping gives −900/13, so replace.
Expected payoff with the test before cost is 0.26(280/13)+0.74(−100/37)=5.6−2.0=3.6.
Subtract the test cost 2: net expected payoff=1.6. Since 1.6 exceeds the no-test value −8, the test is worthwhile by 9.6 expected units.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Bayes' theorem and total probability.
Expected payoff after a signal uses posterior state probabilities.
Net test value=expected payoff with test before cost−test cost.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Checks prior and test branch probabilities, calculates both posteriors, optimizes actions separately by signal, and subtracts the test cost before comparing with the no-test strategy.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A fully labeled decision tree is acceptable if every chance branch sums to one and each decision node selects the higher conditional expected payoff.

common_errors.misconception: Using the sensitivity 0.90 as P(D|+)
corrective_followups: Is sensitivity P(+|D) or P(D|+)?
Which prior and false-positive rate are needed for Bayes' theorem?

common_errors.misconception: Ignoring the test cost when comparing strategies
corrective_followups: Is 3.6 the gross expected payoff or the net payoff?
What amount must be subtracted on every tested unit?
